factors.factor: Single primary database with a failover-only secondary meant one database handled all load and was a single point of failure, with no load distribution across hosts
factors.evidence: "GitLab.com currently uses a single primary and a single secondary in hot-standby mode. The standby is only used for failover purposes. In this setup a single database has to handle all the load, which is not ideal."

factors.factor: Replication lag and failure from unexpected load: WAL segments were removed before the secondary consumed them, and no WAL archiving was in place, requiring manual resynchronisation
factors.evidence: "The replication failed as WAL segments needed by the secondary were already removed from the primary. As GitLab.com was not using WAL archiving, the secondary had to be re-synchronised manually."

factors.factor: The runbooks and official documentation did not describe that pg_basebackup waits silently for the primary to begin streaming, so the expected behaviour was mistaken for a hang
factors.evidence: "this was not clearly documented in our engineering runbooks nor in the official pg_basebackup document."

factors.factor: Manual destructive operations on production had no safeguards (such as host/role verification or confirmation) to distinguish primary from secondary, so a data directory was removed on the primary instead of the secondary
factors.evidence: "an engineer proceeds to wipe the PostgreSQL database directory, errantly thinking they were doing so on the secondary. Unfortunately this process was executed on the primary instead."

factors.factor: Troubleshooting under time pressure involved untested production configuration changes (raising max_wal_senders), which exposed an unreviewed max_connections value of 8000 and caused a restart failure
factors.evidence: "To resolve this our engineers decided to temporarily increase max_wal_senders from the default value of 3 to 32. When applying the settings, PostgreSQL refused to restart... In our case this was set to 8000. Such a value is way too high, yet it had been applied almost a year ago and was working fine until that point."

factors.factor: Backup procedure silently failed because pg_dump version mismatch was not detected, and cron failure notifications were rejected due to DMARC misconfiguration, so failures went unnoticed
factors.evidence: "the backup procedure was using pg_dump 9.2, while our database is running PostgreSQL 9.6... This in turn resulted in pg_dump terminating with an error." and "DMARC was not enabled for the cronjob emails, resulting in them being rejected by the receiver. This means we were never aware of the backups failing, until it was too late."

factors.factor: Disaster recovery reliance on snapshots not designed for DR and on slow, cheap storage, which prolonged recovery
factors.evidence: "The LVM snapshots are primarily used to easily copy data from our production environment to our staging environment... the produced snapshots are not really meant to be used for disaster recovery." and "the disks are very slow, resulting in them being the main bottleneck in the restoration process."

factors.factor: Azure disk snapshots were not enabled for database servers because other backup procedures were assumed to be sufficient, leaving a gap in backup coverage
factors.evidence: "While enabled for the NFS servers, these snapshots were not enabled for any of the database servers as we assumed that our other backup procedures were sufficient enough."

factors.factor: A background job deleting a falsely flagged account added database load during an already stressed period, and spam-based user removal used hard delete without safeguards
factors.evidence: "part of the load was caused by a background job trying to remove a GitLab employee and their associated data. This was the result of their account being flagged for abuse and accidentally scheduled for removal."

action_items.action: Enable WAL archiving (continuous archiving to object storage) for the production PostgreSQL cluster so replicas can recover from WAL segments removed from the primary without manual resynchronisation.
Fix the pg_dump backup job to use a client binary matching the production PostgreSQL major version, and add an automated check that fails the job when versions mismatch.
Route all cron and backup failure notifications through a monitored channel with DMARC-compliant sending, and alert when no successful backup has completed within the expected window.

Add safeguards to production database operations, such as hostname and role verification scripts or confirmation prompts, so destructive commands like removing a data directory cannot run against the primary by mistake.
Enable Azure disk snapshots for all database servers, consistent with the NFS servers, and document their restore time expectations.
Update engineering runbooks to document that pg_basebackup waits silently for the primary to begin streaming replication data, and note expected output and wait times.

Require that configuration changes such as max_wal_senders and max_connections be validated in staging and documented with rollback steps before being applied to production, and review existing values such as the max_connections setting of 8000.
Change account-deletion behaviour for spam-flagged users to soft delete with a review and recovery window, and add throttling for background deletion jobs so they cannot add large database load.
Define and document a disaster recovery plan that does not depend on staging snapshots, including target recovery time objectives and faster storage for restore paths.

Add a documented incident-response step, owned by the incident response process, requiring a second responder to verify the target host and role before any irreversible production command is run during an active incident, and confirm the step is included in the on-call runbook.
Evaluate deploying a read replica load-balancing layer so the primary is not the sole database serving all traffic, reducing the blast radius of load spikes.
